newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb defense concerned about publicity.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb defense concerned about publicity.

text.p: Defence attorneys in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Wednesday charged that Timothy McVeigh's first appearance in public after his arrest was aimed at garnering publicity and had endangered him.

McVeigh's attorney, Stephen Jones, told reporters after a pre-trial hearing that McVeigh's appearance, known as the "perp walk" which was captured by television cameras and broadcast widely and repeatedly, was both dangerous and aimed at attracting as much media coverage as possible.
"They tried to keep him from seeing an attorney, they tried to keep him from making telephone calls ... and they wanted to bring him out in a dramatic fashion," Jones said.

"Of course it wasn't safe. That testimony was almost an insult to one's intelligence," he said, referring to FBI special agent James Adams who told the court he never thought to furnish McVeigh with a bullet-proof vest for the move.

Adams also said McVeigh's move was not delayed in order to give the media time to arrive. Government attorney Aitan Goelman denied that authorities wanted to attract media attention and said the FBI was concerned about safety and took steps to make sure McVeigh was as well protected as possible"
Jones also told reporters he was becoming increasingly troubled by prosecution witnesses allegedly changing or adding to their accounts of events that purportedly linked McVeigh to the bombing.
"I can understand that may happen occasionally ... For it to become the order of the day is becoming very distrubing and I'm not quite sure what's going on here, but I don't like it," he said.
Jones has contended that several prosecution witnesses have in recent months altered their recollection after meeting with prosecutors.
In the second day of a pre-trial hearing on whether certain prosecution eyewitnesses will be allowed to testify, FBI agents supported a half dozen witnesses linking McVeigh to the bombing.
FBI agents and sketch artists described a key prosecution witness as "confident" when he identified McVeigh as the man who rented a truck believed to have been used in the Oklahoma bombing.

McVeigh and co-defendant Terry Nichols are accused of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City in April 1995, killing 168 people. McVeigh's trial begins on March 31 and Nichols will be tried at a later date.
Jury summonses were sent out this week to 1,000 people for the trials, but jurors will not be sequestered, officials said Wednesday.
"That doesn't mean we'll call that many (for jury selection), but we're looking to (having) a big jury panel," James Manspeaker, spokesman for the bombing case judge, said.
The number of summonses sent was the largest ever in Denver federal court, Manspeaker said.
